name: The Biopsychosocial Model
what: This subtopic covers George Engel's biopsychosocial model as a holistic, interdisciplinary framework that considers biological, psychological, and social factors as interacting influences on both mental wellbeing and psychological development.
why: The biopsychosocial model provides a practical and comprehensive tool for analysing why individuals differ in their mental health and developmental outcomes, moving beyond single-cause explanations toward an understanding of cumulative, interacting factors.

items.title: I can define the biopsychosocial model and identify who developed it
items.what: The biopsychosocial model, developed by George Engel in 1977, is a holistic, interdisciplinary framework for understanding the human experience in terms of the interaction of biological, psychological, and social factors.
items.why: Knowing the origin and purpose of the model helps students understand why it was developed as an alternative to purely medical or biological approaches to health and development.
items.example: Engel argued that treating a patient with anxiety only with medication ignores the psychological coping strategies and social support networks that also determine whether the person recovers.

items.title: I can define and give examples of biological, psychological, and social factors
items.what: Biological factors are internal genetic or physiological influences such as hormones, sleep, nutrition, and genetic predispositions. Psychological factors are internal mental processes including thoughts, beliefs, emotions, and coping skills. Social factors are external influences from relationships, community, culture, socioeconomic status, and family environment.
items.why: Correctly classifying factors into the three categories is a core skill required for case study analysis and short-answer questions throughout VCE Psychology.
items.example: In the case of Sam (15 years old), his family history of depression is a biological factor, his rumination about his ex-girlfriend is a psychological factor, and the breakup itself is a social factor.

items.title: I can explain how the three biopsychosocial factors interact to influence mental wellbeing
items.what: Mental wellbeing is determined by the combined and interacting influence of biological, psychological, and social factors. No single factor alone is sufficient to cause high or low wellbeing, and disruption in one area affects the others.
items.why: Understanding the interactive nature of the model prevents students from attributing poor mental health to a single cause and supports the logic behind multi-pronged treatment approaches.
items.example: A person with a genetic predisposition to anxiety (biological) who also holds negative beliefs about their own competence (psychological) and has limited social support (social) is at significantly greater risk of poor mental wellbeing than someone with only one of these factors present.

items.title: I can explain why a strictly biological approach to improving mental wellbeing is often insufficient
items.what: Because mental wellbeing is shaped by all three biopsychosocial factors, addressing only the biological dimension, such as prescribing medication, typically leaves psychological and social contributors unaddressed and is therefore unlikely to produce sustained improvement.
items.why: This point is a common exam application requiring students to evaluate treatment approaches and justify why holistic interventions are more appropriate.
items.example: A teenager prescribed antidepressants who continues to experience bullying at school (social) and uses avoidance as a coping strategy (psychological) is unlikely to achieve lasting improvement from medication alone.

items.title: I can apply the biopsychosocial model to explain developmental outcomes
items.what: The biopsychosocial model can be applied to psychological development by identifying how biological, psychological, and social influences from infancy onward accumulate and interact to produce developmental outcomes across the lifespan.
items.why: Applying the model to development rather than just mental wellbeing demonstrates its interdisciplinary nature and is directly assessed in multi-mark questions.
items.example: An infant who is neglected (social) may experience disrupted brain development (biological) and develop low self-esteem (psychological), which then contributes to social isolation and difficulties finding employment in adulthood, illustrating a cascade of interacting biopsychosocial outcomes.

items.title: I can explain why one negative biopsychosocial influence alone is not sufficient to cause maladaptive development
items.what: Developmental outcomes are determined by the sum and interaction of all biopsychosocial influences encountered across the lifespan. A single negative factor can be buffered by positive influences in other domains, and a single positive factor cannot guarantee optimal development on its own.
items.why: This principle is frequently tested in exam scenarios where students must explain why a character who faces adversity in one area can still function well in others.
items.example: Adrian is a 30-year-old who struggles socially but performs well professionally. His positive biological health and psychological sense of job competence buffer the negative impact of his limited social development.
